id: Anna May Wong Stars as Cyborg #86

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The future is as sterile as a robot’s loincloth. I drown my hands in sanitizer until they pucker. Where this soapbox tree germinates, I collect my germs and make a fountain of them. Because yellow is yarrow and soot, and the future, I’ve learned, is no suture. Because where I’m from, these kisses are infections. Because dirt’s ammunition against discipline, the blood fills my clean mouth with dismay. Am I surprised— Hollywood still assumes we are all the bastard children of the same evil dictator? That phosgene and mustard will rack our titanium Maoist husks until some white man with slanty eyes rescues us from our mealy, pliant selves? Am I to wear Dior, wrap my mouth in bloody tulle, before kneeling, bending to kiss a mouth dirtied by Pantone 136? No fucking thanks. Because where I’m from, these kisses are infractions. Darlings, let’s rewrite the script. Let’s hijack the narrative, steer the story ourselves. There’d be a heist, a battle. Audre Lorde would write the script. My leading man would be Bruce. We’d earn our happy ending. Instead, they give me 1981. 2012. Quantum quasars, new dystopia—plutonium wars. We’re not in Polanski’s Chinatown anymore. Yet we still have the same bowl haircuts. Bangs, big bang, a city of fetid promise, new minor galaxy where we cannot touch. Instead our skin is rust and metal. It gratifies the technophile in all of us.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Where, Because

outputs.L1:
The future is as sterile as a robot’s loincloth. I drown my hands in sanitizer until they pucker. Where this soapbox tree germinates, I gather my germs and make a fountain of them. Because yellow is yarrow and soot—and the future, I’ve learned, is no suture. Because where I’m from, these kisses are infections. Because dirt is ammunition against discipline, blood fills my clean mouth with dismay.

Am I surprised? Hollywood still assumes we are all the bastard children of the same evil dictator—that phosgene and mustard will wrack our titanium Maoist husks until some white man with slanty eyes rescues us from our mealy, pliant selves. Am I to wear Dior, wrap my mouth in bloody tulle, then kneel and bend to kiss a mouth dirtied by Pantone 136? No fucking thanks.

Because where I’m from, these kisses are infractions.

Darlings, let’s rewrite the script. Let’s hijack the narrative and steer the story ourselves. There would be a heist, a battle. Audre Lorde would write the script. My leading man would be Bruce. We would earn our happy ending.

Instead, they give me 1981. 2012. Quantum quasars, a new dystopia—plutonium wars. We’re not in Polanski’s *Chinatown* anymore, yet we still have the same bowl haircuts. Bangs, the Big Bang: a city of fetid promise, a new minor galaxy where we cannot touch. Instead, our skin is rust and metal. It gratifies the technophile in all of us.
outputs.L2:
Tomorrow is antiseptic, as barren as the cloth covering a machine’s groin. I soak my hands in disinfectant until the skin wrinkles. Beneath the place where this podium-tree takes root, I gather my microbes and send them spurting upward like water. Yellow means yarrow, ash, and what lies ahead; I now know the future will not stitch anything closed. In the place I come from, every kiss is a contagion. Since filth arms itself against order, blood floods my scrubbed mouth, filling me with dread.

Should I be shocked? Hollywood continues to imagine us as the illegitimate offspring of one shared, monstrous despot. It expects phosgene and mustard gas to torment our titanium Maoist shells until a white man with “slanted” eyes saves us from our bland, yielding selves. Must I dress in Dior and veil my lips with bloodstained tulle, then bow down to kiss a mouth smeared with Pantone 136? Absolutely fucking not. Where I come from, such kisses are violations.

Beloveds, we should replace the screenplay. Let’s seize control of the plot and drive the tale in our own direction. Our version would include a robbery and a war. Audre Lorde would be the screenwriter. Bruce would play opposite me. We would fight for—and deserve—our joyful conclusion.

But what we receive instead is 1981, then 2012: quantum quasars, another dystopian age, wars fueled by plutonium. Polanski’s *Chinatown* is no longer where we are, though the bowl cuts remain unchanged. Fringe, the Big Bang, and a reeking city that promises everything: a small new galaxy in which touching is forbidden. Our bodies become corroded iron and machinery instead, satisfying the technology lover buried within each of us.
outputs.L3:
The speaker portrays the future not as a place of freedom or possibility, but as a sterile dystopia governed by fear. In this imagined world, contamination is treated as a constant threat, and physical contact becomes dangerous or forbidden. Kisses, intimacy, and human connection are framed as infections or infractions—violations of a social order obsessed with cleanliness, discipline, and control. As a result, the body is no longer a source of warmth or connection; it becomes something regulated, metallic, alienated, and untouchable.

This futuristic vision also exposes the persistence of racism in popular culture, particularly in Hollywood’s representations of Asian people. The text condemns stereotypes that portray Asians as a uniform mass: submissive, emotionless, authoritarian, or incapable of shaping their own destinies. Such narratives often deny Asian characters individuality and agency, while positioning white figures as necessary rescuers or heroes. Although the settings may appear technologically advanced, the stories themselves continue to reproduce old prejudices. Progress in machines, cities, and visual effects does not necessarily lead to progress in the way marginalized people are represented.

Against these dehumanizing narratives, the speaker calls for marginalized communities to reclaim authorship. Rather than accepting roles imposed on them by dominant culture, they must rewrite the stories that have excluded, simplified, or objectified them. This means creating characters who are complex, autonomous, and heroic, as well as imagining futures in which intimacy and human connection are not treated as threats. By telling their own stories, marginalized people can move beyond narratives of victimhood or rescue and claim the right to create their own victories, romances, and happy endings.
outputs.L4:
The speaker presents the future not as a realm of progress and possibility, but as a sterile dystopia built from the prejudices of the past. Images of contamination, bodily vulnerability, artificial environments, and invasive technology create a world in which intimacy has been replaced by fear and human beings are reduced to objects, threats, or data. Although this world appears futuristic, its social logic is deeply familiar: racism, exclusion, and the policing of racialized bodies continue beneath the surface of technological advancement.

The poem particularly challenges the Orientalist stereotypes popularized by Hollywood and other Western cultural industries. Asian identities are imagined through a narrow set of fantasies—as exotic, dangerous, inscrutable, hypersexual, diseased, or mechanically efficient. These representations deny people complexity and agency, turning them into scenery or symbols within someone else’s vision of the future. By drawing on historical references and visceral imagery, the speaker shows that science-fiction narratives often do not invent new worlds at all. Instead, they project old colonial fears and racial hierarchies into new settings.

Contamination anxiety becomes one of the poem’s central metaphors. Fear of disease, touch, mixture, and bodily contact reveals a larger fear of difference. Technology appears to promise cleanliness, control, and protection, yet it also intensifies isolation and dehumanization. In such a future, bodies are monitored, categorized, and kept at a distance, while genuine connection becomes increasingly difficult. The language of safety and progress therefore conceals systems that decide which lives are valued, which bodies are considered dangerous, and who is permitted to belong.

Against this dystopian vision, the speaker insists on the importance of reclaiming storytelling. If dominant narratives repeatedly cast marginalized people as aliens, villains, victims, or disposable figures, then self-authored representation becomes a form of resistance. Telling one’s own story means refusing inherited stereotypes, recovering erased histories, and imagining identities that are not defined by the expectations of others. It also means challenging the assumption that the future must reproduce the violence of the present.

Ultimately, the poem argues that technological novelty alone cannot create liberation. A genuinely different future requires new ways of seeing and relating to one another. By exposing how supposedly futuristic stories recycle racism, Orientalism, and fear, the speaker calls for narratives grounded in agency, memory, vulnerability, and mutual recognition. Only through the power to represent themselves can marginalized people imagine a future in which intimacy is possible, humanity is preserved, and liberation means more than surviving inside an updated version of the past.
outputs.L5:
**The Place Where We Belong**

The road was long, but she kept walking toward the distant lights. She knew where they would lead: home. Not merely a house, but the place where memories lived and familiar voices waited.

She returned because some bonds cannot be broken by time or distance. Because love leaves a path behind us. And because, wherever life may take us, the heart remembers the way back.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, politically charged prose poem critiquing Hollywood’s racist depictions of Asian people in dystopian science fiction, using imagery of sterility, disease, chemical warfare, fashion, and futurism.
counterfactuals.output:
Hollywood builds the future in a disinfected room, then smears yellow light across the windows and calls it Asia. The city is always raining, always diseased with neon; every sign is an unreadable fever, every face an omen arranged behind glass. White heroes move through the crowd in surgical coats, immaculate as alibis, while Asian bodies become atmosphere—steam, static, contagion, a market of interchangeable ghosts.

In the costume department, fear is tailored beautifully. Silk is cut into warning flags. Eyeliner sharpens the enemy. A mandarin collar rises like a quarantine wall. Somewhere, a producer sprays tomorrow with pesticide and asks why the extras are coughing.

The script says the future has no borders, but the camera patrols them. It turns a woman into a hologram, a man into a hive, a language into decorative noise. It calls the metropolis “overcrowded” while giving the chosen hero an empty sky. It calls technology alien when Asian hands assemble it, salvation when a white hand switches it on.

Above the studio lot, drones release a fine cinematic powder: one part opium dream, one part laboratory plague, one part ancient menace upgraded with chrome. The cloud enters every franchise. It settles on the moon. It stains the androids. Even centuries from now, the villain’s palace smells of incense and chemical weapons.

But beneath the sterile future, something living scratches at the set. The faceless crowd removes its masks. The hologram refuses to flicker on cue. Seamstresses unpick the uniforms of empire and resew them into impossible garments—jackets with ten thousand sleeves, gowns that project banned histories, helmets blooming with mouths.

Then the neon characters step down from the billboards and rewrite themselves. The rain stops performing. The city, no longer a symptom, looks back at the lens.

For the first time, Hollywood is the thing under examination: pale beneath the operating lamp, infected with its own imagination, begging the future not to notice how old its nightmares are.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental spoken-word monologue from the perspective of an Asian woman rejecting orientalist stereotypes and reclaiming control of her cinematic narrative. Reference Audre Lorde, Bruce Lee, Chinatown, and Pantone 136.
counterfactuals.output:
**FINAL CUT: PANTONE 136**

No—  
don’t cue the gong.

Don’t steam the glass,  
don’t lacquer my silence,  
don’t dress the camera in red  
and call the lighting *mystery*.

I know this set.

I know the Chinatown built on a backlot,  
every alley folded into somebody else’s fantasy—  
neon grammar, counterfeit moon,  
a dragon curling around the white hero’s plot.

You want me framed in the doorway:  
lotus, dagger, porcelain question mark.  
You want my mouth subtitled  
before I have spoken.

Cut.

I said: **cut.**

Audre Lorde taught us  
silence was never going to protect us,  
so I take mine out of storage,  
crack it open,  
find a voice inside sharpening itself.

Not your exotic.  
Not your obedient.  
Not your tragic little bridge  
between East and West—  
as though I were infrastructure,  
as though I did not have a destination of my own.

Bruce Lee enters the archive  
like water refusing the shape of a stereotype.  
No cardboard mystic.  
No ornamental fist.  
A body thinking at full speed,  
breaking the frame that tried to contain it.

I learn from that motion:

be water, yes—  
but remember water directs ships,  
carves stone,  
returns the city’s false reflection  
to darkness.

Look at me.

No, not like that.

Look again.

This skin is not a filter.  
Not “golden,” not “saffron,”  
not a metaphor waiting for empire.

The colorist holds up **Pantone 136**  
and asks if this is close enough.

Close enough to what?

A warning sign?  
A paper sun?  
The coward’s stripe  
painted across a century of film?

I take the swatch from his hand.

Pantone 136:  
not diagnosis,  
not destiny—  
a small square of color  
I can use or refuse.

Today I make it the sunrise  
behind my own title card.

My name appears first.

My mother keeps her accent  
and gets the final line.  
My grandmother survives the third act.  
The women in Chinatown lock the souvenir shops,  
step out of the establishing shot,  
and inherit the street.

No one translates their laughter.

The camera does not crawl up my body.  
It meets my eyes  
and learns to stay there.

I am not asking for a better cage.  
I am not auditioning for complexity.  
I am not grateful  
to be upgraded from victim to assassin.

I am writing the scene  
where I eat when I’m hungry,  
rage without becoming a dragon,  
love without becoming a lesson,  
leave without being punished,  
return without being forgiven.

Roll sound.

Roll history backward  
until the yellowface peels away,  
until the archive admits  
how many of us were present  
but cropped out.

Now roll forward.

No incense.  
No fetish.  
No borrowed philosophy  
whispered over a white man’s awakening.

Just breath.

Mine.

Just the lens.

Mine.

Just the ending—

No, not ending.

Door opening.  
Street noise.  
A woman walking beyond genre,  
beyond Chinatown’s painted gate,  
beyond Pantone’s numbered borders.

She turns toward the camera.

She does not bow.

She says:

I am not your symbol.  
I am the director.

And this time,  
when I disappear from the frame,

it is because  
I called the cut.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, fragmented prose poem about contamination, forbidden intimacy, anti-Asian racism, and techno-dystopia. Use recurring lines beginning with “Because where I’m from,” along with wordplay, rhetorical questions, and an angry, defiant tone.
counterfactuals.output:
Because where I’m from, the air arrives pre-owned—factory breath, wildfire lung, a soft gray firmware updating the sky without consent.

Because where I’m from, they ask *Where are you really from?* as if my face were a leak in the border, as if ancestry were contraband tucked beneath the tongue.

Contaminate: con + taminate—together we stain. Together, forbidden, our mouths breach protocol. Your hand in mine: an unauthorized device. Your pulse: malware. Kiss me again. Corrupt the clean file they made of us.

Who gets called viral? Who gets to spread?  
A rumor wears yellow skin; a nation coughs; the cameras swivel toward my mother.  
Mask on, mask off—either way they say they can’t read me.  
Either way they read me as threat.

Because where I’m from, love is quarantined by category: race-box, sex-box, citizen-box, check one, check none, check yourself at the checkpoint.

The city scans our fevered faces. **MATCH NOT FOUND.**  
Good.  
We were never meant to match their master image.

Because where I’m from, “smart” means the streetlights know who to dim for, the drones know which surnames to circle, the algorithm learns prejudice in six languages and calls itself neutral.

Neutral—new-tral—new trial, same sentence.

Your apartment glows blue with appliances listening. The refrigerator records our hunger. The mattress monetizes our sweat. Somewhere a server farm blooms like mold, feeding on every forbidden tenderness: thumbprint, timestamp, gasp.

Are we safe?  
Safe for whom?  
Safe like sealed meat? Safe like silence? Safe like a neighborhood scrubbed of every face that makes the property value nervous?

Because where I’m from, they made “Asian” a blade with no handle: model minority, foreign menace, quiet worker, dirty carrier—hold it any way and bleed.

I refuse quiet.  
I refuse clean.

Call me contaminated: I have touched the histories you buried. Rail ties, camps, laundries, islands, exclusion acts lacquered over with apps. I have kissed across your color line. I have put my unapproved body beside another unapproved body and made a small electric riot.

Because where I’m from, intimacy is evidence.

So archive this:  
our mouths unsanctioned,  
our names mispronounced but unmuted,  
our skin refusing the soft erasure of the screen.

The future keeps buffering. The police cloud never forgets. Every door has an eye now, every eye a landlord, every landlord a little god demanding facial recognition.

Recognize this face.

No, closer.

Recognize what your machine cannot digest: I am not your outbreak, your obedient export, your fetish with subtitles. I am the error multiplying inside the empire’s pristine code.

Because where I’m from, survival is not purity.

It is spore. It is static. It is touch after curfew.  
It is us, cross-wired and furious, kissing under the sterilizing lamps—

and when the system asks, **ARE YOU SURE?**

we answer:

**infected with each other.**  
**infected with memory.**  
**infected, yes—**

**and coming through.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine an Asian American heroine criticizing a futuristic Hollywood film that casts her people as robotic Maoist villains awaiting rescue by a white man. Have her demand a rewritten script involving a heist, a battle, and a hard-won happy ending.
counterfactuals.output:
The heroine stood beneath the studio’s holographic billboard, where a square-jawed white savior loomed over a faceless army of Asian drones.

“No,” she said, tearing the script in half. “We are not your robotic Maoist horde. We are not a billion identical bodies waiting for one white man to teach us freedom.”

She tossed the pages onto the conference table.

“Here’s the rewrite: We’re the protagonists. A crew of Asian and Asian American thieves breaks into the regime’s orbital treasury to steal the quantum ledger that keeps every citizen under surveillance. The heist goes wrong—not because we’re obedient machines, but because we disagree, betray each other, make impossible choices, and still find a way back.”

She pointed to the final act on the story board.

“Then comes the battle. Not a massacre of anonymous yellow uniforms—a real fight, led by people with names, families, rivalries, jokes, and scars. We defeat the dictatorship ourselves. Your white hero can help if he wants, but he doesn’t get the crown, the kiss, or the last word.”

She picked up a marker and wrote across the ending:

**THE CITY SURVIVES. THE CREW COMES HOME.**

“And yes, we get a happy ending,” she said. “Not an easy one. We lose friends. We rebuild block by block. We argue over what freedom should look like. But the lovers reunite, the children see daylight, and nobody sails in from the West to save us.”

She capped the marker.

“If Hollywood wants our faces in its future, then it can make room for our humanity there too.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde literary passage blending pandemic-era sanitation anxiety with critiques of yellow peril imagery, cinematic orientalism, and dehumanizing cyberpunk aesthetics. Make the language lyrical, abrasive, profane, and packed with unexpected metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
At the supermarket entrance, the sanitizer dispenser stood like a petty white god, squirting absolution into every upturned palm. We rubbed until our lifelines blurred. We scrubbed the door handles, the apples, the coins, the little plastic windows through which strangers’ eyes flickered like trapped weather. Cleanliness became a border patrol with a lemon scent.

Meanwhile, the old posters woke beneath the city’s skin: the clawed yellow hand around the globe, the slanted shadow creeping under civilization’s bedroom door. Yellow peril—history’s cheap carnival mask, lacquered in cowardice—was dragged from the imperial basement and stapled to the face of a virus. On television, maps bloomed red over Asia as if geography itself had developed a rash. Every cough acquired an accent. Every body became a customs declaration.

Cinema had rehearsed this shit for decades: the gong trembling before anyone entered the room; silk curtains breathing conspiracy; neon ideograms raining down like decorative malware. The East was always a corridor, a code, a dragon-shaped excuse for the white hero to discover his soul. Women arrived as perfume with knives. Men arrived as swarms, masterminds, inscrutable furniture. Nobody was allowed the vulgar miracle of being boring.

Then cyberpunk came, chrome-toothed and masturbating under billboards. It stole Tokyo’s light, Hong Kong’s vertical fever, Seoul’s electric veins, and called the theft “the future.” Asian faces multiplied in the scenery while Asian people vanished from the story. Kanji burned beautifully above noodle stalls where no one had a childhood. Crowds pulsed below like circuitry—anonymous, obedient, infinitely replaceable. A whole continent reduced to set dressing for some trench-coated bastard’s existential hangover.

During quarantine, I watched the city disinfect its conscience. Elevators smelled of hospitals and panic. Neighbors flinched from one another with the choreography of magnets turned wrong-side out. A masked woman on the train was not a woman but a headline wearing shoes. A delivery rider was not a man but an app with wet lungs. We had uploaded prejudice into the contactless interface and congratulated ourselves on innovation.

Fuck the antiseptic myth that fear is neutral. Fear has a wardrobe department. Fear knows where to point the camera. It powders the old caricature, adjusts the dragon’s teeth, adds rain and holograms, then whispers: *Look—danger, but make it cinematic.*

I wanted to take a wire brush to the screen. I wanted to scrape away every exotic skyline until the pixels bled ordinary mornings: grandmothers bargaining over pears, teenagers failing algebra, fathers snoring on sofas, nurses peeling masks from bruised faces. I wanted the future returned to the people forced to decorate it.

Outside, ambulances stitched red thread through the dark. Inside, we washed our hands again—twenty seconds, thirty, forty—until guilt foamed between our fingers. But history is not a surface, and hatred is not grease. No soap reaches the machinery behind the image. You have to break the projector. You have to drag its imperial gears into daylight, coughing dust and celluloid, and ask why the monster always looks foreign while the camera remains innocent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
